So preparations for the pilot began in November of 2020 and as we noted in the report and again the presentation today is just a supplement that written report.

There's been extensive preparations done in order to ensure that we have a successful pilot that we're ready to go and that we've been able to learn from the experiences of other Canadian police agencies.
Starting with that stakeholder engagement has been a key focus thrown and noted by by other agencies as well as our own experience that it is a critical piece to the program and the pilot.
We've done that through a combination of meetings, information sessions, and media and presentations both inside and outside the service.
Internally we conduct the service by the impact analysis to try and gauge what processes, what units, what we're close to be affected by the introduction of cameras.

Policy and procedure development began very early on and again as I know it has been built on the experience of other Canadian police agencies are stakeholder engagement sessions as well as research from academia out of Queen's University.
The policy has been reviewed by the federal provincial crown privacy commissioner of Saskatchewan.
The public committee gave me public complaints commission in Saskatchewan Human Rights and this is Saskatchewan Police Association.
Our policy and procedure was also kind of circulated and we have some key FAQs on that on our website.

Moving forward, the project team will handle all the training and has been done by Sergeant Gracie since then.
As far as the pilot itself goes we have 40 cameras out of a possible 265 uniform positions that could wear cameras and the first cameras hit the street on April 4th, 2022.
Today we have received very positive feedback both from the members wearing cameras, other members on shift who don't have a camera, investigators executive and partners.

Starting in April we did a very gradual rollout and that has been kind of a key theme and a lesson from other agencies is that we move gradually we move mindfully so that we can ensure that we can handle the impact and our partners can as well.
The gradual rollout also helped to ensure that any technical issues, any support that the members required using the cameras was there and that we had the time before we rolled all 40 out.

By early May all 40 were an operation. The pilot itself is made up of members from across the service a number of different units and a number of different shifts and cameras are deployed on each shift throughout the city.

We looked at the members for the pilot we wanted to ensure that we got to mix of both those that were tech savvy and very excited about the program as well as those that would probably need a little bit more support in using those.
So we have a good cross section of our membership in the pilot.
Finally, today we've spent approximately 190,000 on the hardware and software licenses for the first year licensing costs are annual and hardware of course is a one-time capital expense.
